name.text: Evaluating an Integral by parts-question 1 test quiz

generalfeedback.text:
Worked out solution

The first step here is to pick \(u\) and \(dv\) so that when we compute \(du\) and \(v\) and plugging everything to have:

\( \displaystyle \int udv = u \cdot v - \int vdu\)

With that in mind it looks like the following choices for \(u\) and \(dv\) should work for us:

\(u = {@func_var_u@}\), \(dv ={@func_var_dv@} dx\), therefore,
Next, we need to compute \(du\) (by differentiating \(u\)) and \(v\) (by integrating \(dv\)).

\(du = \displaystyle {@diff_u@}\, dx\) and \(v= \displaystyle {@int_v@}\)

Plugging the above into the Integration by Parts formula gives:

\( \displaystyle \int ({@func_var_u@}){@func_var_dv@} dx = ({@func_var_u@})\cdot({@int_v@}) - \displaystyle \int ({@int_v@}){@diff_u@} \,dx\)


The new integral we get is easily doable, let's focus on it as shown:

\(\displaystyle \int ({@int_v@}){@diff_u@} \,dx= {@int_v_du@} + c\), therefore replacing it back we’ll get:

\( \begin{align} \displaystyle \int ({@func_var_u@}){@func_var_dv@} \, dx & = ({@func_var_u@})\cdot({@int_v@}) - \displaystyle \int ({@int_v@}){@diff_u@} dx \\ & = {@ta@} \end{align}\)

where \(c\) is constant of integration.
